rationale: Interpreted the shutdown-race receipt and corrected my first reading of its comparison outcomes: the outcomes labelled violated for the verify case mean one evaluated trial contradicted the assertion, not that all of them did, and the underlying events show the predicted hang in two of three trials (9 and 41 of 64 futures left uncompleted against 0 in the control). The question is therefore explained rather than refuted: VerifyLeader futures can be stranded by a concurrent Shutdown, the mechanism is the buffered verifyCh plus a future without a shutdown channel, the exposure is timing dependent, and Barrier and Apply did not show it in the same run, which is consistent with the different drain patterns. A Fact records the observation with its indices; no execution is requested this turn.

knowledge.statement: A VerifyLeader future handed back while Shutdown is in progress can be left permanently uncompleted, because the request sits in the buffered verifyCh that the exiting run loop never drains and the future has no shutdown channel of its own to unblock on. In the retained run: 9, 41 and 0 of 64 calls per trial were still incomplete 400ms after Shutdown() returned (50 of 192 overall), every completed call returned success, and the no-shutdown control completed 64 of 64; Barrier and Apply never left a future incomplete in the same run (0 of 192 each), consistent with applyCh being drained in batches while verifyCh is drained one case per iteration.
knowledge.conditions: Single-voter Raft instance with HeartbeatTimeout = ElectionTimeout = LeaderLeaseTimeout = 50ms, 64 concurrent calls issued before Shutdown() is called, in-memory transport in one process; Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets state Shutdown, and verifyCh is buffered with 64 slots.

interpretations.rationale: The question was whether a future handed back by VerifyLeader, Barrier or Apply while Shutdown runs can be left permanently uncompleted, and the execution answers yes for VerifyLeader. In the retained run of three shutdown trials (result events at parsed indices 1, 7 and 13) the verify cases left 9, 41 and 0 of their 64 futures uncompleted 400ms after Shutdown() had returned, with every completed call reporting success; the same call kind on a node that is never shut down completed all 64 in its control (index 19). So 50 of 192 verify calls were still waiting long after the node had reported Shutdown complete, and nothing is left that could answer them: Shutdown closes shutdownCh and sets the state to Shutdown (api.go 1060-1072), the run loop and the FSM goroutine both exit on that channel, and the futures sit in verifyCh, a buffered channel of 64 (api.go 576) that nobody drains afterwards. That matches the source: VerifyLeader creates a verifyFuture and calls init(), which allocates only the error channel (future.go 99-101), leaving ShutdownCh nil, so deferError.Error() waits on errCh or on a channel that is never used (future.go 103-117). The contract names ErrRaftShutdown as an error a client may see from these calls, and the repository's own test file already carries a TODO that Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration can get stuck when the buffered channel consumes a future that shutdown then never processes (raft_test.go 38-42). The exposure is timing dependent rather than uniform: the third verify trial left nothing behind, and the run's other two call kinds never left a future incomplete at all (Barrier 0 of 192 across indices 3, 9, 15; Apply 0 of 192 across 5, 11, 17). That difference is consistent with how the loop drains each channel: it takes one case per iteration from verifyCh, whereas applyCh is drained in batches up to MaxAppendEntries in the group-commit loop, so a queue of apply or barrier futures is emptied before the shutdown case is chosen far more reliably. The mechanism itself does not require many callers: any single VerifyLeader whose send wins the select while the loop is exiting lands in the buffer and stays there, but the likelihood that the buffer is non-empty at that moment grows with concurrent callers, which is what the probe exercises.
counterevidence: One of the three verify trials left no future uncompleted, and the two other call kinds never did in 384 attempts, so the outcome is a race whose probability depends on queue occupancy at the exit rather than a deterministic property of the API.

The repository's test file records the same class as a known TODO for Barrier, VerifyLeader and GetConfiguration, which is a source admission that the gap exists rather than a contract that permits it; it is cited here as evidence about intent, not as a reason to withhold the finding.
Every future that did complete in these trials reported success, so the hang is confined to calls that were never served; no completed call was answered with a wrong outcome.
limitations: The probe deliberately uses 64 concurrent VerifyLeader calls to make queue occupancy likely; it does not measure the probability for a single call racing Shutdown, only that the race exists.
The single-voter configuration removes commit latency as a confounder but also means verify requests need no peer round trip, so nothing else can be holding the queue.

Whether a stuck future could ever be answered later is inferred from the source and from the node reporting Shutdown complete with no loop running; the harness waited 1500ms per call and 400ms after Shutdown returned, not indefinitely.
The counts varied widely across trials (9, 41, 0), so the true rate is not bounded by this execution.
